XI.1.title: The rustics of former times
XI.1.reflection: In ritual and music, people say, the earlier generations were rustic and the later ones refined gentlemen. If Confucius had to choose, he would follow the earlier. He prefers plain sincerity to elaborate polish.
XI.1.question: In your own field, do you prefer the older plain way or the newer refined one?

XI.2.title: The four lists
XI.2.reflection: None of those who were with him in Chen and Cai, where he and his followers nearly starved, now come to his door. The second part, probably added by the compilers, lists the most famous disciples under four headings: virtue, speech, government and culture. It is the oldest roll of the school.
XI.2.question: Under which of the four headings would your friends place you?

XI.3.title: Hui is no help to me
XI.3.reflection: Hui is no help to me; he is pleased with everything I say. Half complaint and half praise: a teacher learns from objections, and Hui never made any.
XI.3.question: Who helps you most by disagreeing?

XI.4.title: What others say of him
XI.4.reflection: Min Ziqian is filial indeed: no one finds anything to object to in what his parents and brothers say of him. A family's praise is often partial; here even outsiders agree.
XI.4.question: Would outsiders agree with what your family says of you?

XI.5.title: The white jade sceptre
XI.5.reflection: Nan Rong often recited an ode about a flaw in a white jade sceptre that can be polished away, while a flaw in speech cannot. Confucius gave him his niece in marriage. A man who repeats a warning about careless words shows his own care.
XI.5.question: What line do you repeat to yourself as a warning?

XI.6.title: No one loves learning now
XI.6.reflection: Ji Kangzi asks which disciple loved learning, the question Duke Ai asked in VI.2. The answer is the same, shorter: Yan Hui, and he died young; now there is no one. The repetition carries the grief.
XI.6.question: What quality of someone you lost has no one else replaced?

XI.7.title: The outer coffin
XI.7.reflection: When Yan Hui died, his father asked for the Master's carriage to sell for an outer coffin. Confucius refused: everyone speaks of his own son, gifted or not; when my son Li died he had no outer coffin either, and as one who follows the officials I cannot go on foot. Even grief does not override what he thinks his position requires.
XI.7.question: When has propriety asked you to refuse something you wanted to give?

XI.8.title: Heaven is destroying me
XI.8.reflection: When Yan Hui died, the Master said: alas, Heaven is destroying me, Heaven is destroying me. The disciple he hoped would carry on his Way is gone. The book does not soften the cry.
XI.8.question: Whose loss would feel like losing part of your own work?

XI.9.title: If not for him, for whom?
XI.9.reflection: Confucius wept for Yan Hui without restraint, and his followers said his grief was excessive. Is it? If not for this man, for whom should I grieve? The teacher of measure refuses measure here.
XI.9.question: Is there a grief you have been told was excessive that was not?

XI.10.title: A grand funeral against his wish
XI.10.reflection: The disciples wanted a grand funeral for Hui; the Master said no, since Hui's family was poor. They gave him one anyway. Hui treated me as a father, Confucius says, and I could not treat him as a son; it was not my doing, it was yours. Even in mourning, he wanted the form to match the truth.
XI.10.question: When have others honoured someone in a way that person would not have wanted?

XI.11.title: Life before death
XI.11.reflection: Zilu asks about serving the spirits. Not yet able to serve people, how can you serve spirits? He asks about death. Not yet understanding life, how can you understand death? The answer is not denial but order of priority.
XI.11.question: What question about the end are you asking before you have answered one about the present?

XI.12.title: The disciples around him
XI.12.reflection: Min Ziqian at his side looked respectful, Zilu bold, Ran You and Zigong frank and easy, and the Master was pleased. Then: as for Zilu, he will not die a natural death. Zilu later died in a coup in Wei. A happy scene ends with a foreboding.
XI.12.question: What do you see in a friend's temperament that worries you?

XI.13.title: Why rebuild?
XI.13.reflection: The people of Lu were rebuilding the Long Treasury. Min Ziqian asks: why not keep the old one? Why must it be rebuilt? Confucius says: this man seldom speaks, but when he does he hits the mark. The rebuilding may have been a show of power by the families.
XI.13.question: What are you about to replace that could simply be kept?

XI.14.title: In the hall, not yet in the room
XI.14.reflection: Zilu's playing of the zither was too martial for the Master's door, and when he said so, the other disciples stopped respecting Zilu. Confucius corrects them: Zilu has ascended the hall, though not yet entered the inner room. A rebuke is not a dismissal.
XI.14.question: When did a criticism of someone make others think less of them than it should have?

XI.15.title: Too far is like not far enough
XI.15.reflection: Zigong asks who is better, Zizhang or Zixia. Zizhang goes too far, Zixia not far enough. Then Zizhang is better? Going too far is as bad as falling short. The doctrine of the mean in one sentence.
XI.15.question: Where are you going too far, believing it is better than falling short?

XI.16.title: No disciple of mine
XI.16.reflection: The Ji family was richer than the Duke of Zhou had been, and Ran Qiu still collected taxes to make it richer. He is no follower of mine; you may beat the drums and attack him. The harshest disowning in the book is for helping the powerful take from the people.
XI.16.question: Have you ever helped someone with more than enough take still more?

XI.17.title: Four disciples in a word
XI.17.reflection: Chai is simple, Shen is slow, Zizhang is showy, Zilu is coarse. Four disciples, each summed up in a word. Shen is Zengzi, who in other chapters speaks as a master; being called slow did not stop him.
XI.17.question: What one word would a teacher of yours have used for you?

XI.18.title: Often empty
XI.18.reflection: Hui was near the Way and often in want. Zigong did not accept his lot and made money in trade, and his guesses were often right. Confucius sets the poor disciple beside the prosperous one without condemning the second.
XI.18.question: Can one be good at making money and still near the Way?

XI.19.title: The good man
XI.19.reflection: Zizhang asks about the good man, shan ren. He does not follow in others' tracks, but he does not enter the inner room either. Natural goodness without learning goes some way, not all the way.
XI.19.question: How far can goodness without study take a person?

XI.20.title: Solid talk
XI.20.reflection: If we approve of someone because their talk is earnest, is that a junzi, or someone who only looks serious? The chapter warns against judging character by tone.
XI.20.question: Whose earnest manner have you trusted too quickly?

XI.21.title: Two answers to one question
XI.21.reflection: Zilu asks whether to act at once on what he hears; he is told to consult his father and elder brothers first. Ran Qiu asks the same and is told to act at once. Gongxi Chi is puzzled. Ran Qiu holds back, so I urged him on; Zilu has the energy of two, so I held him back. The book's clearest example of teaching fitted to the student.
XI.21.question: Which advice do you need today: to act now, or to wait and ask?

XI.22.title: While you live
XI.22.reflection: In the danger at Kuang, Yan Hui fell behind, and the Master said: I thought you were dead. While you are alive, Hui replied, how would I dare die? Devotion, and a touch of humour, under threat.
XI.22.question: For whom would you stay alive, if you could choose?

XI.23.title: Great ministers or ordinary ones
XI.23.reflection: Ji Ziran, of the Ji family, asks whether Zilu and Ran Qiu, who serve the Ji, are great ministers. A great minister serves his lord by the Way and resigns when he cannot; these two are ordinary ministers. Then they will do whatever they are told? Not if told to kill a father or a ruler. The answer is a warning to the family itself.
XI.23.question: What would you refuse to do for an employer, whatever the order?

XI.24.title: Learning before governing
XI.24.reflection: Zilu has the young Zigao made governor of Bi. You are harming someone's son, says Confucius. Zilu argues: there are people to govern, altars to tend; why must one read books first? That is why I dislike clever talkers. Putting someone unready into office harms them as well as the people.
XI.24.question: Have you been put into a role before you were ready, or put someone else there?

XI.25.title: Bathing in the Yi
XI.25.reflection: Four disciples tell their wishes. Zilu would save a besieged state in three years; Ran Qiu would make a small state prosperous; Gongxi Chi would be a minor assistant at ritual. Zeng Xi lays down his zither and wishes, in late spring, to bathe in the river Yi with a few friends and boys, enjoy the breeze at the rain altars and come home singing. The Master sighs: I am with Dian. It is the book's longest scene, and it ends with a picture of contentment.
XI.25.question: What would your wish be, if asked in the same circle?
XI.25.exercise: Spend a few minutes today outside, simply enjoying the air, as Zeng Xi wished to.
